title: Custom Hooks
summary: **Custom Hooks** are plain JavaScript functions whose names start with `use` that let you extract and reuse stateful logic between components — without changing your component hierarchy.

subtopics.title: The use* naming rule
subtopics.explanation: A function only counts as a Hook if its name starts with `use`. This isn't decoration: the `use` prefix is the signal the React linter and React itself rely on to apply and enforce the Rules of Hooks. Name a function `getData` and call useState inside it and the linter can't protect you; name it `useData` and it can.

subtopics.title: Composing built-in hooks
subtopics.explanation: A custom Hook is built by calling useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, or even other custom Hooks inside it and combining them into one named behavior. There is no special machinery; it is ordinary function composition over the built-in primitives. This composability is what lets a useFetch Hook layer useState for data, useEffect for the request, and useRef for cancellation.

subtopics.title: Returning tuples vs objects
subtopics.explanation: Return a tuple [value, setValue] when callers should be free to rename the results, mirroring useState. Return an object { data, loading, error } when there are several named results or some are optional, since named destructuring is self-documenting and order-independent. The rule of thumb: two-value, rename-friendly returns lean tuple; multi-value or extensible returns lean object.

subtopics.title: Sharing logic vs sharing state
subtopics.explanation: This is the single most misunderstood point: custom Hooks share logic, never state. Two components calling the same useCounter each get their own independent count because the Hooks inside register state on each caller's own fiber. If you actually need shared state, lift it to a common parent or back the Hook with Context; the Hook itself never creates a shared store.

subtopics.title: Stable references inside hooks
subtopics.explanation: Functions and objects a custom Hook returns are recreated on every render unless you memoize them. If a caller puts a returned function in a dependency array or passes it to a memoized child, an unstable identity defeats that memoization and can cause extra effect runs. Wrap returned callbacks in useCallback and derived objects in useMemo when they feed dependency arrays.

subtopics.title: Cleanup and dependencies
subtopics.explanation: Because a custom Hook embeds effects, it carries the same lifecycle obligations as inline Hooks: correct dependency arrays and cleanup functions. A useFetch must cancel or ignore stale requests on unmount or when the URL changes, and a useEventListener must remove its listener. Forgetting this turns a convenient Hook into a leak that ships everywhere the Hook is used.

subtopics.title: Common hook patterns
subtopics.explanation: A handful of custom Hooks recur in nearly every codebase: useToggle for boolean UI state, useFetch/useQuery for remote data with loading and error flags, useLocalStorage for persisted state, useDebounce for smoothing rapidly-changing values, and useMediaQuery for responsive logic. Knowing these by heart is interview table stakes because they exercise composition, cleanup, and return-shape decisions all at once.

foundations.overview: A custom Hook is just a function that calls other Hooks. When two components need the same stateful behaviour — fetching data, reading from localStorage, debouncing a value — you copy that logic into a function whose name starts with `use`, and call it from each component. The components stay clean and the logic lives in one tested place.
foundations.formalDefinition: A custom Hook is a JavaScript function whose name begins with `use` and that calls one or more React Hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef, or other custom Hooks). It encapsulates reusable stateful logic and returns values for the calling component to use.
foundations.whyItMatters: Custom Hooks are React's primary mechanism for sharing non-visual logic. They replaced older, clunkier patterns (higher-order components and render props) with a flat, composable, easy-to-test approach, which is why nearly every production React codebase has a hooks/ folder.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a custom Hook as a recipe, not a shared pot of soup. Every component that calls the Hook follows the same recipe but gets its own fresh, independent batch of state. You are sharing the logic, never the data.
foundations.browserPerspective: Custom Hooks add no new browser primitive. At runtime they are ordinary function calls; the Hooks they call inside still register state and effects on the calling component's fiber. The DOM only ever sees the result of the component that used the Hook.
foundations.realWorldUsage: useFetch for data loading, useLocalStorage for persisted settings, useDebounce for search inputs, useToggle for modals and switches, useMediaQuery for responsive logic, useForm for form state — these are staples of real apps and component libraries.
foundations.businessImpact: Extracting logic into custom Hooks reduces duplicated, drifting code. Fewer copies of the same fetch-and-error logic means fewer bugs in features that touch revenue, and faster delivery of new screens that reuse proven behaviour.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Custom Hooks make stateful logic unit-testable in isolation and let teams build a shared vocabulary of behaviours. They keep components focused on rendering while the 'how' lives in well-named, reusable functions.
foundations.performanceImpact: A custom Hook has the same render cost as inlining its Hooks — it adds no overhead by itself. Care is still needed: effects and derived values inside the Hook re-run on the caller's renders, so dependency arrays and memoisation matter just as they would inline.
commonUseCases: useFetch / useQuery wrappers for loading remote data with loading and error flags
useLocalStorage / useSessionStorage to persist and sync state with storage
useDebounce / useThrottle to smooth rapidly-changing values like search input
useToggle / useDisclosure for boolean UI state (modals, dropdowns, accordions)

commonMisconceptions.myth: Two components calling the same custom Hook share the same state.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They do not. Each call gets its own independent state — the Hook shares the logic, not the values. To share state, lift it up or use Context.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A custom Hook is special React magic.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is an ordinary function. The only thing that makes it a Hook is the `use` prefix (so the linter and React can apply the Rules of Hooks) and the fact that it calls other Hooks.

visualExplorer.title: Extracting logic into a custom Hook
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through turning duplicated useState + useEffect logic into one reusable use* function that each component calls independently.

config.intro: A custom Hook is built by lifting Hook calls out of a component into a use* function. Follow the lifecycle of that extraction.

steps.name: Spot the duplication
steps.detail: Two components both call useState and useEffect to do the same thing (e.g. read/write localStorage). That repeated logic is a candidate for extraction.

steps.name: Create a use* function
steps.detail: Move the Hook calls into a new function named with the use prefix, e.g. function useLocalStorage(key, initial) { ... }. The prefix tells React and the linter to enforce the Rules of Hooks.

steps.name: Accept inputs as arguments
steps.detail: Parameterise what differs between callers — the storage key, an initial value, a URL — so the Hook is generic and reusable.

steps.name: Return values to the caller
steps.detail: Return a tuple [value, setValue] (like useState) or an object { data, loading, error } so the component can read the results.

steps.name: Call it from each component
steps.detail: Replace the duplicated code with one line: const [name, setName] = useLocalStorage('name', ''). Each component now follows the same recipe.

steps.name: Each call is independent
steps.detail: Every component that calls the Hook gets its own fresh state and effects. The logic is shared; the data is not.

interactiveExamples.title: useToggle: a tiny reusable Hook
interactiveExamples.explanation: We extract boolean-toggle logic into useToggle. It calls useState internally and returns the value plus a toggle function. Notice the Hook is defined above App and called like any built-in Hook.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A button that toggles a paragraph on and off using the reusable useToggle Hook.

interactiveExamples.title: Each call gets its own state
interactiveExamples.explanation: Two counters both use the same useCounter Hook, yet their values are completely independent. This proves custom Hooks share logic, not state.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Two independent counters; incrementing one does not affect the other.

interactiveExamples.title: useDebounce: composing useState + useEffect
interactiveExamples.explanation: useDebounce returns a value that only updates after the input has stopped changing for a delay. It composes useState and useEffect, cleaning up the timer between renders.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The debounced value lags the live value until you stop typing for half a second.

codeLab.title: Build useLocalStorage
codeLab.instructions: Write a custom Hook useLocalStorage(key, initialValue) that reads the initial value from localStorage (falling back to initialValue), keeps it in state, and writes back to localStorage whenever it changes. Return [value, setValue] so it behaves like useState. Use it in App to persist a name across reloads.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Typing a name persists it — reloading the preview keeps the saved value.
hints: Use a lazy initializer: useState(() => localStorage.getItem(key) ...) so it reads storage only once.
Use useEffect with [key, value] to write to localStorage whenever the value changes.
Return the [value, setValue] tuple so callers can use it just like useState.

debuggingLab.title: useFetch refetches forever
debuggingLab.symptom: The component flickers and the network tab shows the same request firing in an endless loop.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The useEffect inside useFetch has no dependency array, so it runs after every render. Each fetch calls setData, which triggers a re-render, which runs the effect again — an infinite fetch loop.
commonMistakes: Omitting the dependency array on an effect that updates state.
Putting a freshly-created object or array in the dependency array, which is a new reference every render.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add the correct dependency array so the fetch only runs when the url changes.

theory.question: What is a custom Hook and what makes a function a Hook?
theory.directAnswer: A custom Hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with `use` and that calls one or more React Hooks. The `use` prefix is what makes it a Hook: it tells React and the linter to enforce the Rules of Hooks. Its purpose is to extract and reuse stateful logic between components.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An ordinary function that composes built-in Hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef, or other custom Hooks) to package reusable behaviour.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Before Hooks, sharing stateful logic required higher-order components or render props, which added wrapper layers and were hard to compose. Custom Hooks share logic with a flat, simple function call.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The Hook runs as part of the calling component's render. The Hooks it calls register state and effects on that component's fiber, so each component that calls the Hook gets its own independent state.

theory.whyImportant: Custom Hooks are the idiomatic way to avoid duplicated logic in React. Interviewers use them to check whether you understand composition, the Rules of Hooks, and the difference between sharing logic and sharing state.
theory.realWorldExample: A useFetch Hook holds data, loading, and error state and runs the request in an effect, so any screen can load data with one line.

nestedTopics.title: The use* naming rule
nestedTopics.explanation: Names must start with use so the linter can verify that Hooks are only called at the top level of a component or another Hook.

nestedTopics.title: Composing built-in Hooks
nestedTopics.explanation: A custom Hook is built by calling useState, useEffect, useRef and others inside it, combining them into one behaviour.

nestedTopics.title: Sharing logic vs sharing state
nestedTopics.explanation: Each component calling the Hook gets its own state. To share the actual values, lift state up or use Context.

followUps.question: Do two components calling the same Hook share state?
followUps.answer: No. They share the logic but each gets its own independent state. Sharing values requires lifting state up or using Context/a store.

followUps.question: Can a custom Hook call another custom Hook?
followUps.answer: Yes. Hooks compose freely — a custom Hook can call useState, useEffect, and other custom Hooks, as long as it follows the Rules of Hooks.

theory.question: Should a custom Hook return a tuple or an object, and why?
theory.directAnswer: Return a tuple [value, setValue] when callers should be free to rename the values (mirroring useState), and return an object { data, loading, error } when there are several named results or some are optional. Tuples favour renaming; objects favour clarity and optional fields.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A design decision about the shape of a custom Hook's return value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different consumption patterns suit different shapes. Tuples let callers pick their own names; objects self-document each value and avoid ordering mistakes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: With a tuple, callers destructure by position (const [a, setA] = useThing()), so they choose the names. With an object, callers destructure by key (const { data, loading } = useThing()), so the names are fixed but self-explanatory.

theory.whyImportant: API design of Hooks is a common discussion point; it signals whether you think about how others will consume your code.
theory.realWorldExample: useState returns a tuple so you can name a thousand pieces of state distinctly; useQuery returns an object because { data, isLoading, error, refetch } are clearer by name.

nestedTopics.title: Positional vs named destructuring
nestedTopics.explanation: Tuples are positional, objects are named — choose based on how many values there are and whether callers need to rename them.

nestedTopics.title: Stable function references
nestedTopics.explanation: Returned functions may need useCallback so they stay stable across renders for use in dependency arrays.

nestedTopics.title: Optional return fields
nestedTopics.explanation: Objects make it easy to add optional fields later without breaking existing destructuring positions.

followUps.question: When does a returned setter need useCallback?
followUps.answer: When callers put it in a dependency array or pass it to memoised children; useCallback keeps the reference stable so effects and memoisation behave.

followUps.question: Can you mix both styles?
followUps.answer: Yes, but it is rare — usually pick one. A tuple with a trailing object of extras is sometimes seen but can confuse consumers.

scenario.question: Two sibling components call your useCart() Hook, but updates in one are not reflected in the other. The team expected them to stay in sync. What is happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Each call to useCart() creates its own independent state, so the two components hold separate carts. Custom Hooks share logic, not state. To share the actual cart, lift the state into a common parent and pass it down, or expose it through React Context (e.g. a CartProvider) and have the Hook read from that Context.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A misunderstanding of the difference between reusing logic and sharing state.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The Hooks a custom Hook calls register state on the calling component's own fiber, so two callers get two separate states.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: To share one source of truth, the state must live in a single place above both components — a shared parent or a Context provider — and the Hook must read from that shared location rather than calling useState itself.

scenario.whyImportant: This is the single most common misconception about custom Hooks; interviewers use it to confirm you understand React's data flow.

nestedTopics.title: Lifting state up
nestedTopics.explanation: Move the state to the closest common ancestor and pass it down via props.

nestedTopics.title: Context-backed Hooks
nestedTopics.explanation: A Hook can call useContext to read state shared by a provider, giving every consumer the same data.

followUps.question: When is independent state actually what you want?
followUps.answer: Most of the time — useToggle, useDebounce, useForm are meant to be per-component. Shared state is the special case, not the default.

coding.question: Implement a useToggle Hook that returns the current boolean and a function to flip it, then use it to show/hide a panel.
coding.thoughtProcess: Toggle logic is just a boolean in useState plus a flip function. I keep the boolean in state, expose a stable toggle that uses the functional updater so it never reads stale state, and return them as a tuple so it reads like useState.
coding.lineByLine: useState(initial) holds the boolean. toggle uses the functional updater setOn(o => !o) so it always flips the latest value. The Hook returns [on, toggle] as a tuple, mirroring useState so callers can name them freely.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a single boolean of state.

alternativeApproaches.title: Return extra setters
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Return { on, toggle, setOn, setTrue, setFalse } as an object when callers need explicit open/close actions, not just a flip.

followUps.question: Why use the functional updater inside toggle?
followUps.answer: So the flip is always based on the latest value, avoiding stale-closure bugs if toggle is called multiple times in one event.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep custom Hooks in a dedicated hooks/ folder, one Hook per file, named use*. Keep each Hook focused on a single concern and compose them rather than building one giant Hook. Push side effects (fetching, storage) into Hooks so components stay declarative.
productionDeepDive.performance: A custom Hook costs the same as inlining its Hooks. The risks are the same too: missing or unstable dependency arrays cause extra effect runs, and returned functions/objects that change identity every render can defeat memoisation. Use useCallback/useMemo inside the Hook when its results feed dependency arrays.
productionDeepDive.security: Hooks that touch storage or the network must treat all returned data as untrusted and avoid persisting secrets to localStorage, which is readable by any script on the page. Validate and sanitise before use.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As the app grows, a small library of well-named Hooks (useFetch, useLocalStorage, useDebounce) becomes shared infrastructure. Version and document them like any internal package; breaking their return shape ripples across many call sites.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Name Hooks for behaviour, not implementation. Co-locate their tests. Because the logic is isolated, you can unit-test a Hook (with a testing library's renderHook) without rendering a full component.
productionDeepDive.observability: React DevTools shows custom Hooks and their internal state in the component inspector, so you can see exactly what a Hook is holding at runtime and trace unexpected re-renders to a specific Hook.

caseStudies.problem: Data-fetching logic (loading, error, abort) was copy-pasted into a dozen components and drifted out of sync.
caseStudies.solution: Extracted a single useFetch Hook with consistent loading/error handling and request cancellation, then replaced every copy with one call.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A small upfront abstraction cost vs eliminating a recurring source of bugs.
caseStudies.lessons: Extract a Hook the moment the same stateful logic appears in a second place; one tested implementation beats many drifting copies.

projectBuilder.summary: Add a small library of custom Hooks that power the dashboard's interactive pieces — persisting filters, debouncing search, and loading data.
requirements: A useLocalStorage Hook that persists the user's chosen filters
A useDebounce Hook that smooths the search input
A useFetch Hook that loads the user list with loading and error flags
projectBuilder.architecture: Create a hooks/ folder with one file per Hook. The UsersTable composes them: useFetch loads rows, useDebounce smooths the search term before filtering, and useLocalStorage remembers the status filter between sessions.
projectBuilder.folderStructure:
src/
  hooks/
    useFetch.js
    useDebounce.js
    useLocalStorage.js
  components/
    UsersTable.jsx
    SearchBar.jsx

steps.title: Build useDebounce
steps.instructions: Create useDebounce(value, delay) using useState + useEffect with cleanup, and use it to debounce the search box.
steps.checkpoint: Filtering only runs after the user stops typing.

steps.title: Build useLocalStorage
steps.instructions: Create useLocalStorage(key, initial) and back the status filter with it.
steps.checkpoint: The selected filter survives a page reload.

steps.title: Build useFetch
steps.instructions: Create useFetch(url) returning { data, loading, error } and use it to load the users table.
steps.checkpoint: The table shows a loading state, then data, and handles errors.

enhancements: Add request cancellation to useFetch with AbortController
Add a useMediaQuery Hook to switch the table to a card layout on mobile
interviewQuestions: Why does each component that calls useDebounce get its own debounced value?
How would you make useFetch cancel an in-flight request when the url changes?

keyTakeaways: A custom Hook is a function named use* that calls other Hooks to package reusable stateful logic.
Custom Hooks share logic, not state — every call gets its own independent state.
Compose built-in Hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef) and other custom Hooks freely, following the Rules of Hooks.
Return a tuple [value, setValue] when callers should rename values, or an object for several named results.
Extract a Hook as soon as the same stateful logic appears in a second component — one tested copy beats many drifting ones.
